prompts.title: Every state's income tax as data (2025, 2026)
prompts.effort: One agent, about 15 minutes (or 26 small helpers, two states each, in a couple of minutes)
prompts.value: Puts every state's income tax rules (all 50 states and DC, 2025 and 2026) into the app as data, each figure from the state's own tax department. The State tax page cannot be built without it, and state tax is often thousands of dollars a year in every take-home and retirement figure.
prompts.summary: All 50 states and DC in one data file, every figure from the state's own revenue department.
prompts.text:
# Every state's income tax as data (2025, 2026)

You are improving **Financial Planner**, an open-source personal finance app: https://github.com/luisitin/financial-planner (branch `main`, MIT licence).
Plain ES modules, Node 20, no framework, no bundler. One page = one folder `modules/<group>/<id>/` holding `module.js` (manifest),
`compute.js` (pure math: runs in the browser, on the PC server and in tests), `view.js` (DOM only), `README.md` (purpose,
formulas with sources) and `module.test.mjs` (node:test). Shared math lives in `core/math/`. The plan is one JSON object
(`docs/DATA_MODEL.md`). The owner reads the app on a 390 px phone and is not a finance professional: words on screen are plain.

**Read these first** (raw files you can fetch directly; the whole repo is at https://github.com/luisitin/financial-planner):
- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/luisitin/financial-planner/main/docs/DATA_MODEL.md
- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/luisitin/financial-planner/main/modules/taxes/state/README.md
- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/luisitin/financial-planner/main/modules/taxes/state/module.js
- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/luisitin/financial-planner/main/core/math/tax.js
- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/luisitin/financial-planner/main/modules/taxes/federal/data/federal.js

## The task

The planned State tax page (`taxes/state`) needs each state's personal income tax as data. Produce `modules/taxes/state/data/states.js` for all 50 states and the District of Columbia, tax years 2025 and 2026, in exactly this shape:

```js
export const STATES = {
  CA: {
    2025: {
      kind: "brackets",            // "brackets" | "flat" | "none" | "interest-dividends-only" | "capital-gains-only"
      brackets: { single: [[0, 0.01], [10756, 0.02]], married_joint: [...], married_separate: [...], head_of_household: [...] },
      standard: { single: 5540, married_joint: 11080, married_separate: 5540, head_of_household: 11080 },   // 0 if none
      exemption: { personal: 149, dependent: 461, kind: "credit" },   // "deduction" or "credit"
      startsFrom: "federal-agi",   // "federal-agi" | "federal-taxable" | "own"
      retirement: { socialSecurityTaxed: false, pensionExclusion: null },   // the state's retirement-income rules, with limits
      notes: ["mental health services tax: 1% over $1,000,000"],   // anything the simple model leaves out
      source: "https://... (the revenue department's own rate schedule or form instructions)",
    },
    2026: { ... },
  },
  TX: { 2025: { kind: "none", source: "..." }, 2026: { kind: "none", source: "..." } },
};
```

Rules:
- Every number comes from the state's revenue department (rate schedule or form instructions), never an aggregator. Where 2026 is not yet published, carry 2025 forward and add `"projected: not yet published"` to `notes`.
- States that cut rates on a schedule or a revenue trigger (for example Arkansas, Georgia, Indiana, Iowa, Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, Missouri, Nebraska, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, South Carolina, West Virginia): note the schedule and the trigger.
- Local income taxes (New York City, Yonkers, Maryland counties, Pennsylvania and Ohio localities, Michigan cities, Indiana counties, Kansas City and St. Louis) go in `notes`; they are not modelled.
- Washington's capital-gains excise tax and New Hampshire's interest-and-dividends tax (for the years it applies) get their own `kind`.

Then add `tests/state-tax-data.test.mjs`: the shape for every state and year, brackets ascending, rates between 0 and 15%, and one hand-worked return per state that has an income tax. If your tool can run helpers, give each two states; one agent alone is fine too.

## How to hand it back

- **If you can work in the repo** (Codex, Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Jules, Copilot's coding agent, or any tool connected to GitHub): make the changes on a new branch `ai/quick-state-tax-tables` from `main`, run `npm test` and `npm run check`, commit with `Prompt: quick-state-tax-tables` on its own line in the message, push the branch and open a pull request against `main`. The repo is public, so commit only under the GitHub no-reply identity the commits on `main` use, never under a personal name or email: before your first commit, run `git config user.name "$(git log -1 --format=%an origin/main)"` and `git config user.email "$(git log -1 --format=%ae origin/main)"`. The pull request's description holds your rationale, the files you touched, the commands you ran and `Prompt: quick-state-tax-tables` on its own line. Do not merge it. If your tool opens the pull request for the owner (Codex's "Create PR" button), end your last message with `Prompt: quick-state-tax-tables` so it reaches the description. The owner's board picks the pull request up within the hour; nothing else is needed.
- **If you cannot push** (a chat): put everything in your reply, as below. The owner pastes your reply into their board.

## How to answer

1. Start with a rationale of at most ten lines: what you changed and why.
2. Give the data as a whole JavaScript module (`export const ...`), each figure with a source comment, in a fenced block whose first line is `// path: <where it goes>`; then the tests that use it, as a unified diff or whole file.
3. A whole file goes in its own fenced code block whose first line is a comment with its path (`// path: modules/x/y/compute.js`).
4. End with the list of files you touched and the commands that verify them (`npm test`, `npm run check`).

Rules:
- Follow the project's rules in `AGENTS.md`: `compute.js` stays pure (no DOM, fetch, storage or timers); money math lives in code, never in an AI model; plain words on screen; every formula gets a test and a written source.
- Never edit `modules/registry.js` (generated by `npm run registry`), `data/` or `planner.properties`.
- Tests use `node:test` and `node:assert/strict`, in the module's `module.test.mjs` or `tests/<topic>.test.mjs`, so that `npm test` and `npm run check` stay green. Say which commands you ran; if you could not run them, say so plainly.
- Every number needs a source (IRS/SSA/CMS publication, statute, paper, or a worked example you show). Put the source next to the number in a comment and in the module README.
- The repo is public: use invented example data only (no real names, addresses, account numbers).
- If something is unclear, state your assumption and carry on; do not stop to ask.

# Federal income tax for 12,000 invented returns (2024 to 2026)

You are improving **Financial Planner**, an open-source personal finance app: https://github.com/luisitin/financial-planner (branch `main`, MIT licence).
Plain ES modules, Node 20, no framework, no bundler. One page = one folder `modules/<group>/<id>/` holding `module.js` (manifest),
`compute.js` (pure math: runs in the browser, on the PC server and in tests), `view.js` (DOM only), `README.md` (purpose,

- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/luisitin/financial-planner/main/modules/taxes/federal/data/federal.js
- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/luisitin/financial-planner/main/modules/taxes/federal/README.md
- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/luisitin/financial-planner/main/modules/taxes/federal/compute.js
- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/luisitin/financial-planner/main/tests/tax.test.mjs
- https://raw.githubusercontent.com/luisitin/financial-planner/main/core/csv.js

## The task

The federal tax engine (`federalTax(inputs, params)` in `core/math/tax.js`, year tables in `modules/taxes/federal/data/federal.js`) has a few dozen hand-worked tests. Give it twelve thousand.

**Scope: what the engine covers** (the README's "Edge cases" lists what it leaves out; do not test those): tax years 2024, 2025 and 2026; single, married filing jointly, married filing separately, head of household; wages, taxable interest, ordinary and qualified dividends, short- and long-term capital gains and losses (with the $3,000 loss limit), pensions and IRA distributions, Social Security benefits (the taxable-portion worksheet), the standard deduction with the 65+ and blind additions, the 2025 to 2028 senior deduction and its phase-out, itemized deductions (state and local taxes under that year's cap, mortgage interest, charity), the child tax credit and the credit for other dependents with their phase-outs, the 3.8% net investment income tax and the 0.9% additional Medicare tax.

**Step 1, the lead (about 10 minutes).**
- Read the input and output objects of `federalTax` and fix one CSV layout: `case_id, year, filing_status, age_1, age_2, blind_1, blind_2, kids_under_17, other_dependents, wages, interest, ordinary_dividends, qualified_dividends, st_gain, lt_gain, pensions, ira_distributions, social_security, salt_paid, mortgage_interest, charity`, then the expected results `agi, taxable_social_security, deduction, taxable_income, ordinary_tax, capital_gains_tax, credits, niit, additional_medicare, total_tax, marginal_rate`, then `note`.
- Write one rules sheet with each year's figures copied from the IRS's own documents: Rev. Proc. 2023-34 (2024), Rev. Proc. 2024-40 plus the July 2025 law's changes (2025), Rev. Proc. 2025-32 (2026). It covers brackets, standard deductions and additions, capital-gains thresholds, Social Security base amounts, credit amounts and phase-outs, the NIIT and additional Medicare thresholds, the SALT cap and its phase-down, and the senior deduction. Wherever `federal.js` differs from the IRS figure, that difference goes first in your answer.
- Give every worker the layout, the rules sheet and its shard.

**Step 2, the workers (in parallel).** 48 shards: 3 years × 4 filing statuses × 4 income bands (under $50,000; $50,000 to $150,000; $150,000 to $400,000; over $400,000 up to $5,000,000). Each worker writes 250 rows for its shard:
- 100 grid rows, incomes spread evenly through the band, the mix rotating through wages only, wages plus investment income, retirement income (pension, IRA, Social Security) and everything at once;
- 100 edge rows: exactly at, $1 below and $1 above every bracket edge, capital-gains threshold, Social Security base amount, credit phase-out start and end, NIIT threshold, senior-deduction phase-out and SALT phase-down point that falls inside the band;
- 50 random rows, every field drawn at random within the band.

Work each expected value from the rules sheet and the IRS worksheets (Qualified Dividends and Capital Gain Tax Worksheet, Social Security Benefits Worksheet, Schedule 8812, Forms 8960 and 8959). A calculator, or a short script you write yourself from the rules sheet, is fine. **Never run, import or copy the repo's code**: the point is an independent answer key. Use the same rounding in every row (exact cents, or whole dollars as the forms allow) and say which.

**Step 3, the workers.** Re-derive every tenth row a second way (by hand if the first pass was a script, by script if it was by hand). Fix the row, or flag it in `note`.

**Step 4, the lead.**
- Re-derive a 2% sample yourself; redo any shard with an error in it.
- Deliver `tests/golden/taxes/federal-<year>.csv` (one per year) and `tests/golden-federal.test.mjs`. The test reads each CSV with `parseCsv` from `core/csv.js`, maps the columns to `federalTax`'s inputs and asserts every result within $1.

(`docs/DATA_MODEL.md`). The owner reads the app on a 390 px phone and is not a finance professional: words on screen are plain.

## The task

Build an answer key for every formula and rule on these 12 working pages, at volume, as CSV files the tests replay:

- `investments/holdings` (Holdings): What you hold in each investment account, what it is worth and what you paid; type it in or import the brokerage's positions file.
- `investments/allocation` (Allocation): Your mix by asset class across every account against the mix you aim for, and how far each class has drifted.
- `investments/rebalance` (Rebalance): The trades that bring your mix back to its target: new money first, then sells where they cost no tax and buys with the cash freed.
- `investments/fees` (Fees): What your funds and any advisor charge each year and what that costs over a lifetime.
- `investments/performance` (Performance): Your true return from the balance points you save: what the investments earned and what you earned, against the plan and an index mix.
- `investments/dividends` (Dividends): The dividends and interest your holdings pay each year, by fund and by account, and what they cover of your spending.
- `investments/asset-location` (Asset location): Which investments belong in which kind of account to keep the yearly tax bill down, the drag today, and the swaps that fix it.
- `investments/glide-path` (Glide path): How much of your money should be in stocks at each age: the plan's path, the rules of thumb, and where you stand today.
- `investments/risk` (Risk): How rough the ride of your mix is: the worst year and deepest fall history has dealt a mix like yours, in your own dollars.
- `investments/backtest` (Backtest): Any stocks-and-bonds mix run through the years since 1871, side by side with another: growth, the worst years, the deepest fall.
- `investments/tax-lots` (Tax lots and harvesting): The gain or loss on each lot you hold, the losses worth harvesting in taxable accounts, and the order to sell in when you need cash.
- `investments/limits` (Contribution limits): This year's limits for 401(k)s, IRAs, HSAs, FSAs and 529 gifts against what is going in, the room left, the Roth income check and the deadlines.

**Step 2, the workers (one per page; split a big page by formula).** Fill the page's CSV with at least 100 rows per formula or rule:
- 60 grid rows across realistic values: one person and a family, small and large amounts, this year and 30 years out;
- 30 edge rows: zero, empty lists, exactly at every threshold the README names and either side of it, the first and last month or year, leap days, and negative amounts where they can occur;
- 10 extreme rows: very large, very small, very long horizons.

Work each expected value from the brief with your own arithmetic, or a short script you write yourself from the brief.

**Step 3, the workers.** Re-derive every tenth row a second way (by hand if the first pass was a script, by script if it was by hand). Fix the row, or flag it in `note`.

**Step 4, the lead.** Re-derive a 2% sample yourself; redo any page with an error. Deliver `tests/golden/investments/<page>.csv` and one runner, `tests/golden-investments.test.mjs`. 1. Start with a rationale of at most ten lines: what you changed and why.
2. Next, the disagreements between your answer key and the code, each with the worked numbers: they matter most. Then give every CSV file and the test runner whole, each in its own fenced code block whose first line is its path (`# path: tests/golden/...csv`; that line is dropped when the file is saved). If the files add up to more than about 1 MB, attach them instead of pasting: one file each, or one Markdown file holding them all in fenced blocks with their paths.
3. End with the list of files you touched and the commands that verify them (`npm test`, `npm run check`).

- Never run, import or copy the repo's code to get an expected value: the answer key must be independent of the code, or it proves nothing. A calculator, or a short script a worker writes itself from the rules in this prompt, is fine.

- The repo is public: use invented example data only (no real names, addresses, account numbers).
